intro: The Torah, the first five books of the Tanakh, begins with two long books that most readers know at least in pieces: Genesis (Bereshit) and Exodus (Shemot). Genesis moves from the creation of the world to one family and its promises. Exodus follows that family, now a people, out of slavery, to a mountain, and into the building of a tent for God to dwell among them. Together they set up nearly everything the rest of the Tanakh assumes.

In this unit you will read these books the way Jewish tradition reads them, as Torah studied week by week, and the way historians and literary readers read them, as texts from the ancient Near East with a shape, a style and a history. You will meet Rashi and the midrash, the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Code of Hammurabi, the Passover Haggadah and the spiritual "Go Down, Moses." You will not be asked to decide whether the stories are true; you will be asked to say what they say and how their readers have read them.

By the end you will be able to name the parts of Genesis and Exodus in order, explain key terms such as covenant, parashah, Akedah, Aseret HaDibrot and Mishkan, quote passages in the JPS 1917 translation, compare a biblical story with a neighboring ancient text, and describe how the same verses are read differently by Jewish and Christian readers and by historians.
bigQuestion: How do Genesis and Exodus turn the story of a world, a family and a rescue into the covenant that the rest of the Tanakh builds on?

title: Torah: Genesis and Exodus

chapters.title: Genesis: From Creation to Joseph
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the book of Genesis tie a creation story, a flood, and one family's promises into a single thread?

story.title: The Walk Up the Mountain
story.kicker: A father and a son climb a hill with wood, fire and a knife, and the son asks a question that the text never fully answers.
paragraphs: Early in the morning, an old man saddles a donkey. The book of Genesis says his name is Abraham. He cuts wood, wakes two servants and his son Isaac, and sets out for a place called Moriah. The text gives no speech, no argument, no tears. It says only that he rose early and went.

On the third day, Abraham sees the place far off. He tells the servants to wait. He puts the wood on Isaac's back and carries the fire and the knife himself. Genesis 22 says the two of them walked on together. Then Isaac speaks. He says, "Father." Abraham answers, "Here am I, my son."

Isaac asks the question that readers have turned over for more than two thousand years. He sees the fire and the wood. Where is the lamb for the offering? Abraham answers that God will see to the lamb. The text says again that the two of them walked on together. It does not say what either of them was thinking.

Jewish tradition calls this story the *Akedah*, the binding of Isaac. It is read in synagogues on Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. The rabbis of the midrash filled its silences with stories. Modern readers, Jewish and not, have argued about what it teaches and whether Abraham was right to go.

This chapter walks through the whole book of Genesis, called *Bereshit* in Hebrew, from the first words about creation to the last words about Joseph in Egypt. The book moves from the whole world to one family. Along the way it keeps returning to one idea: a promise, and the people who carry it.
story.think: Genesis 22 never says what Isaac was thinking. Why might a storyteller leave that out on purpose, and what does the reader have to do because of it?

lessons.title: Two Ways to Tell a Beginning
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis opens with two accounts of creation, and readers have long noticed that they tell the story in different orders and with different names for God.
reading: The Tanakh begins with the word *Bereshit*, "in the beginning." That word is also the Hebrew name of the whole first book. In English the book is called Genesis, from a Greek word for origin. The first chapter counts off seven days. Light comes first, then sky and sea, land and plants, sun and moon, fish and birds, land animals, and last of all human beings. On the seventh day God rests. Jewish tradition connects that rest to Shabbat, the weekly day of rest.

Then, at Genesis 2:4, the story seems to begin again. This second account is told in a different style. It names God differently, using the four-letter name that JPS 1917 prints as "the LORD." It is not built on days. Here a man is formed from dust before any plants grow, then a garden is planted, then animals are made, and then a woman is formed from the man's side. The order is not the same as chapter 1.

Readers have handled the two accounts in different ways. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, reads the second story as filling in the details of the first. Many modern scholars read them as two separate traditions placed side by side by an editor. Jewish tradition holds both chapters as Torah. In this course we describe the readings; we do not rule on which is right.

One thing both accounts share is *parallelism* of a kind. Ideas are repeated in patterns: "and God saw that it was good" returns like a refrain, and the days pair up, with light on day one and the lights of the sky on day four. Noticing these patterns is the first step of reading Genesis as literature, and Jewish readers have done it for centuries.

words.d: Hebrew for "in the beginning"; the first word and the Hebrew name of the book of Genesis
the English name of the first book of the Torah, from a Greek word for origin
the Jewish day of rest, from Friday evening to Saturday evening, which tradition links to the seventh day of creation

check.q: What does the Hebrew word Bereshit mean?
check.why: Bereshit means "in the beginning"; it is the first word of the Torah and the Hebrew name of Genesis.

check.q: Which of these is a real difference between the two creation accounts in Genesis 1 and 2?

Genesis 1 is a poem in Greek and Genesis 2 is in Hebrew
They put the making of plants, animals and people in different orders
Genesis 2 has seven days and Genesis 1 has none
check.why: Genesis 1 makes plants before people; Genesis 2 forms the man before the garden is planted. The seven days belong to chapter 1.

choices: He says it should be removed from the Torah
He reads it as filling in details of the first account
He says it was written by Moses in Egypt
He says it comes from a Babylonian story
check.why: Rashi reads Genesis 2 as adding detail to Genesis 1, not as a rival story.

lessons.title: The Garden and the First Brothers
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 2 through 4 tells of a garden, a choice, and the first murder, and Jewish readers have drawn lessons about responsibility from each scene.
reading: Genesis 2 places the first humans in a garden called Eden. The text says they may eat from every tree but one, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. A talking serpent tells the woman that eating it will open their eyes. She eats, and gives some to the man. When God asks what happened, the man blames the woman and the woman blames the serpent. They are sent out of the garden.

Jewish tradition does not usually read this scene as a story of "original sin" in the way many Christian readers do. The rabbis of the midrash and later commentators tend to read it as a story about choice and its results. The characters are given the power to decide, and they must live with what they chose. Christian tradition, especially after Augustine, reads it as the moment sin entered all human nature. Both readings begin from the same Hebrew words.

In Genesis 4 the first two brothers, Cain and Abel, bring offerings. The text says God accepts Abel's and not Cain's, without saying why. Cain, angry, kills his brother in a field. When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers with a question that has become famous: "Am I my brother's keeper?" The text then says the voice of Abel's blood cries out from the ground.

The Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code, draws on the word "blood" in that verse. It notes that the Hebrew word is plural, "bloods," and reads it to mean Abel's blood and the blood of all the descendants he would never have. From this the Mishnah teaches that whoever destroys one life is as if he destroyed a whole world. That is a *midrash*: a reading that fills a gap in the text with meaning.

words.d: the garden in Genesis 2 and 3 where the first humans live before they are sent out
a rabbinic way of reading that fills gaps in the text with stories or teachings
the first written collection of rabbinic law, edited c. 200 CE

look.title: Two Readers, One Garden
look.text: Reading A: The garden story shows that people were given a real choice and had to face the results. Its lesson is about responsibility. Reading B: The garden story shows the moment sin entered human nature, which every person is born into. Its lesson is about the need for rescue. Many Jewish commentators lean toward A; many Christian traditions, following Augustine, teach B.
look.prompt: Both readings start from the same words in Genesis 3. Name one detail in the story that each reader might point to for support.

check.q: Which tree were the humans told not to eat from in Genesis 2?
choices: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil
check.why: Genesis 2:17 names the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as the one forbidden tree.

check.q: How does Jewish tradition usually read the Eden story, according to the lesson?
choices: As a story about choice and responsibility
As proof that gardens are holy places
As the moment original sin entered all human nature
As a story that never happened
check.why: Jewish readers generally read Eden as a story about choice and its results; the "original sin" reading belongs mainly to Christian tradition.

check.q: The Mishnah's teaching that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world comes from a close reading of which story?
check.why: The Mishnah reads the plural "bloods" in Genesis 4:10, about Abel, to include all his lost descendants.

lessons.title: Noah's Flood and Gilgamesh's Flood
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis tells of a great flood, and an older Mesopotamian poem tells one too; comparing them shows what is shared and what Genesis says differently.
reading: Genesis 6 through 9 tells of a flood that covers the earth. The text says the world had filled with violence, and God decides to wash it away. One man, Noah, is told to build an ark, a huge wooden boat, and to bring his family and pairs of every animal aboard. Rain falls for forty days. When the water goes down, Noah sends out a raven and then a dove. The dove comes back with an olive leaf. God then makes a *covenant* with Noah and sets a rainbow in the sky as its sign.

In 1872 a scholar named George Smith, working at the British Museum in London, read a broken clay tablet from ancient Nineveh and found a flood story on it. It is part of the Epic of Gilgamesh, a long poem from Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Its hero, Utnapishtim, is warned by a god, builds a boat, saves animals, and sends out birds when the water goes down. The tablet is far older than any copy of Genesis we have.

The two stories share a shape: a warning, a boat, animals, birds, a mountain, an offering. They also differ. In Gilgamesh, many gods argue, and the flood comes because humans are too noisy. In Genesis, one God acts, and the reason is human violence. Genesis ends with a promise never to flood the earth again. Scholars use the older story to understand the world Genesis grew up in. Jewish tradition reads Genesis as Torah regardless of what its neighbors told.

For this course, the point is not to decide which story is "true." It is to see that Genesis was written in a world that already told flood stories, and to notice how the Torah's telling stresses justice, one God, and a covenant. Those are the threads that run through the rest of the book.

a long Mesopotamian poem, older than the Bible, that includes a flood story
the ancient land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in today's Iraq

look.title: Two Floods Side by Side
look.text: Genesis 6–9: one God decides; the reason is violence; Noah builds an ark; rain for forty days; a raven and a dove; the ark rests on a mountain; an offering; a rainbow and a promise. Gilgamesh, tablet XI: the gods decide together; the reason given is human noise; Utnapishtim builds a boat; a storm for days; a dove, a swallow and a raven; the boat rests on a mountain; an offering; the hero is made immortal.

check.q: Who is the flood hero in the Epic of Gilgamesh?
check.why: Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh the flood story on tablet XI of the epic. Noah is the Genesis hero.

check.q: What sign does Genesis say God set as a token of the covenant with Noah?
check.why: Genesis 9 names the rainbow as the sign of the promise never again to flood the earth.

check.q: According to the lesson, what reason does Genesis give for the flood, and what reason does Gilgamesh give?
choices: Genesis: human violence; Gilgamesh: human noise
Genesis: too many people; Gilgamesh: too few
check.why: Genesis 6 speaks of violence filling the earth; in Gilgamesh the gods are disturbed by human noise.

lessons.title: Babel and the Shape of Genesis
lessons.mainIdea: The tower of Babel ends the first part of Genesis, and the book's own structure shows a shift from the whole world to one family.
reading: Genesis 11 tells of a city where all people speak one language. They decide to build a tower with its top in the heavens, to make a name for themselves. The text says God comes down, mixes their language so they cannot understand each other, and scatters them. The city is called Babel. The Hebrew plays on the word for "mixed up." The name also points to Babylon, the great city of Mesopotamia whose tall stepped temples, called ziggurats, were famous.

With Babel, the first eleven chapters of Genesis come to a close. Scholars often call these chapters the primeval history, meaning the story of the earliest world. They move fast and cover the whole human race. Then, at the end of chapter 11, the camera narrows. A family in the city of Ur is named. One of its sons is Abram. From chapter 12 to chapter 50, Genesis follows that one family and no other.

Jewish tradition divides Genesis into twelve weekly readings, each called a *parashah*. Each takes its name from one of its first words. The first, Bereshit, covers creation to Noah. Lech Lecha, "go forth," begins Abraham's story. The last, Vayechi, "and he lived," ends with Joseph's death in Egypt. Synagogues around the world read these portions in the same weeks each year, finishing the whole Torah in a year.

A useful way to hold the book in your head is by its own repeated phrase. Ten times Genesis says "these are the generations of" someone: the heavens and the earth, Adam, Noah, the sons of Noah, Shem, Terah, Ishmael, Isaac, Esau and Jacob. The Hebrew word is *toledot*. Many readers use these headings as the book's table of contents.

words.d: the city in Genesis 11 where the tower is built and language is mixed; the name points to Babylon
one weekly portion of the Torah read in the synagogue; plural parashot
Hebrew for "generations"; a heading Genesis repeats to begin a new family section

look.title: Genesis by the Numbers
look.cite: Genesis, JPS 1917 chapter divisions; parashah divisions as printed in standard Hebrew Bibles
look.prompt: Most of the book is about one family. What does that tell you about what the writers of Genesis most wanted to say?

check.q: What does Genesis say God did at the tower of Babel?
choices: Mixed the people's language and scattered them
check.why: Genesis 11 says the one language was confused and the builders were scattered across the earth.

check.q: What is a parashah?
choices: A weekly portion of the Torah read in synagogue
A Hebrew word for a flood

check.why: Genesis 12 opens with the call to Abram to leave his land; chapters 1–11 cover the early world.

lessons.title: Abraham, Sarah and the Call
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 12 begins with a command to go and a promise of land, people and blessing, and this covenant is the thread the rest of the Tanakh follows.
reading: Genesis 12 opens with a command and a promise. The text says God tells Abram to leave his country, his family and his father's house, and to go to a land that God will show him. In return, God promises to make him a great nation, to bless him, and to make him a blessing. Abram goes. He takes his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and their household, and they travel to Canaan, the land that later becomes Israel.

The promise is repeated and made more exact in later chapters. In Genesis 15, the text says God shows Abram the stars and promises descendants as many as the stars. In Genesis 17, God changes his name to Abraham and Sarai's to Sarah, and gives the sign of the covenant: circumcision, the *brit milah* that Jewish families still keep for baby boys on the eighth day. The word for this bond is *covenant*, and it comes up again and again.

Abraham and Sarah are old and have no children. Sarah laughs when she hears she will have a son. The son is born and named Isaac, which plays on the Hebrew word for laughter. Jewish tradition calls Abraham, Isaac and Jacob the *patriarchs*, the fathers, and Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah the *matriarchs*, the mothers. Many Jewish prayers begin by naming them.

Midrash adds stories the text does not tell. The most famous says that young Abram smashed the idols in his father's shop and blamed the largest one, to show his father that idols cannot act. This story is not in Genesis. It is in a collection called Genesis Rabbah, from the early centuries of the Common Era. Knowing which parts are text and which are midrash is a basic skill in reading the Tanakh.

words.d: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the fathers of the people of Israel in Genesis
Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, the mothers of the people of Israel in Genesis
the covenant of circumcision, given in Genesis 17 and kept by Jewish families on a boy's eighth day

lessons.title: Hagar and Ishmael
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis gives Hagar, Sarah's Egyptian servant, her own encounter with God and her own promise, and readers across traditions have treated her story with care.
reading: Before Isaac is born, Sarah gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham so that a child can be born through her. That was a practice known in the ancient Near East. Hagar becomes pregnant and, the text says, looks down on Sarah. Sarah treats her harshly, and Hagar runs away into the wilderness. Genesis 16 says a messenger of God finds her by a spring. The messenger tells her to go back, and promises that her son will father a great people.

Hagar names God with a name of her own, one that JPS 1917 renders as "Thou art a God of seeing." Readers often note that she is the only person in the Tanakh who gives God a name of her own. Her son is called Ishmael, "God hears." Years later, after Isaac is born, Sarah asks Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away. Abraham is troubled. The text says God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael too will become a nation.

In Genesis 21, Hagar and the boy run out of water in the wilderness. Hagar sets the child under a bush. She sits at a distance so she will not see him die. The text says God hears the boy's voice, and Hagar sees a well. This chapter is read in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, before the Akedah is read on the second. The two readings are paired: two sons of Abraham, each nearly lost, each spared.

Islamic tradition honors Hagar and Ishmael as ancestors of the Arab peoples and of the Prophet Muhammad. The Quran tells of them in its own way. Jewish and Christian readers have often noticed how much sympathy the Genesis text shows for a servant woman treated unfairly. Describing all these readings, without ranking them, is how this course handles a shared story.

the son of Abraham and Hagar; his name means "God hears"
the Jewish New Year, on which Genesis 21 and Genesis 22 are read in synagogue

look.title: A Well in the Wilderness
look.text: Picture a dry valley with low bushes. A woman has set a boy under a bush and walked away, because she cannot bear to watch. Genesis 21 says God hears the boy's voice, a messenger speaks to the woman, and her eyes are opened to a well of water that was there all along. Rashi comments that God judges a person by what they are now, not by what they or their children will do later.
look.prompt: The text says Hagar's eyes were opened to a well. Was the well new, or had she not seen it? What might Rashi's comment add to how a reader understands the scene?

check.q: What does the name Ishmael mean?
check.why: Ishmael comes from the Hebrew for "God hears"; Isaac's name plays on laughter.

check.q: Which chapters are read on the two days of Rosh Hashanah, according to the lesson?
check.why: Genesis 21 (Hagar and Ishmael) is read on the first day and Genesis 22 (the Akedah) on the second.

check.q: What is unusual about Hagar in Genesis 16?
choices: She builds an altar in Egypt
She is the first person to plant a vineyard
She gives God a name of her own, something readers note as rare in the Tanakh
She is the mother of Isaac
check.why: Genesis 16:13 has Hagar give God a name; she is the mother of Ishmael, not Isaac.

lessons.title: The Akedah: Reading the Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 22 tells the binding of Isaac in very few words, and Jewish tradition has read its gaps through midrash, liturgy and argument for two thousand years.
reading: Genesis 22 begins by saying God tested Abraham. God tells him to take his son Isaac to the land of Moriah and offer him there. Abraham rises early and goes. On the mountain he builds an altar, binds Isaac, and lifts the knife. A messenger of God calls out and stops him. Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead. The promise of blessing is repeated. Then Abraham returns to his servants. The text does not say that Isaac returned with him.

The Hebrew word for "binding" gives the story its name, the *Akedah*. Nineteen verses carry an enormous weight. Almost nothing about feelings is stated. The rabbis of the midrash noticed this and filled the gaps. One midrash has Abraham arguing with God about the contradiction between this command and the promise. Another has Isaac asking to be bound tightly so that he will not flinch. These are not in the text; they are readings of it.

Rashi reads the command "take thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac" as a slow conversation. Abraham says he has two sons; God says the only one; Abraham says each is the only son of his mother; God says the one you love; Abraham says he loves both; and only then does God say Isaac. Rashi's point is that the text piles up words to show the command being given gently, one step at a time.

The Akedah is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and the shofar, a ram's horn, is blown on that holiday. Tradition connects the horn to the ram in the thicket. Jewish thinkers of the modern era have read the story in opposite ways: as the highest picture of trust, or as a warning that a voice commanding harm to a child must be questioned. Christian tradition often reads Isaac carrying the wood as a picture of Jesus carrying the cross. Each reading begins from the same nineteen verses.

words.d: Hebrew for "binding"; the story of the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22
a ram's horn blown on Rosh Hashanah; tradition links it to the ram in Genesis 22
Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105), the most widely read Jewish commentator on the Torah

look.title: The Command
look.text: And He said: 'Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.'
look.prompt: Rashi hears four steps in this one verse: thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, Isaac. What changes for a reader who hears it as a slow conversation rather than a single blunt order?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word Akedah mean?
check.why: Akedah means "binding," from the verb used when Abraham binds Isaac in Genesis 22:9.

check.q: How does Rashi read the phrase "thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac"?
choices: As a slow, step-by-step conversation between God and Abraham
As a mistake by a later scribe
As proof that Abraham had only one son
As a quotation from the Epic of Gilgamesh
check.why: Rashi imagines Abraham answering each phrase, so the command is given gently in stages.

check.q: What is blown on Rosh Hashanah that tradition links to the Akedah?
check.why: The shofar is a ram's horn, and tradition connects it to the ram caught in the thicket in Genesis 22.

lessons.title: Rebekah, Jacob and Esau
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 25 to 28 tells how the younger twin, Jacob, gets the birthright and the blessing, and readers have long debated how the text judges him.
reading: Isaac marries Rebekah, whom Abraham's servant finds at a well in Genesis 24. Rebekah is barren for years, then carries twins who struggle inside her. The text says God tells her that two nations are in her womb and that the elder will serve the younger. The first twin is born red and hairy and named Esau. The second comes out holding his brother's heel and is named Jacob, a name that plays on the word for heel.

Esau grows up a hunter; Jacob stays near the tents. One day Esau comes in from the field starving and sells his birthright, the older son's share, to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. Later, when Isaac is old and blind, Rebekah helps Jacob dress in Esau's clothes and goatskins, and Jacob receives the blessing meant for Esau. Esau's cry when he learns the truth is one of the most painful lines in Genesis. Jacob flees to his uncle Laban.

Readers have judged Jacob very differently. Some midrashim make Esau a villain so that Jacob's actions look justified. Other readers, ancient and modern, note that the text itself never praises the trick. Jacob will later be deceived by Laban, who swaps a bride in the dark, just as Jacob deceived his father in the dark. Many readers see the text quietly balancing the scales.

On the road to Laban, Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a ladder set on the earth with its top in heaven and messengers of God going up and down. The text says God repeats the promise given to Abraham. Jacob names the place Beth-El, "house of God." This scene is read in synagogues in the parashah called Vayetze, "and he went out."

words.d: the special share and standing of the firstborn son, which Esau sells to Jacob
Isaac and Rebekah's older twin, a hunter, who loses the birthright and the blessing
"house of God," the place where Jacob dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven

look.title: Does the Text Judge Jacob?
look.text: Scene 1 (Genesis 27): In the dark of blindness, Jacob wears his brother's clothes and says "I am Esau." His father gives him the blessing. Scene 2 (Genesis 29): In the dark of night, Laban gives Jacob his older daughter Leah instead of Rachel. In the morning Jacob asks, "Wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban answers that in his country the younger is not given before the firstborn.
look.prompt: The narrator never says Jacob did wrong. Do you think the second scene is the text's way of judging the first? What clues support your view?

check.q: What did Esau sell to Jacob for a bowl of stew?
check.why: Genesis 25 says Esau sold his birthright, the firstborn's share, for red lentil stew.

check.q: What does Jacob's name play on in Hebrew?
check.why: Jacob was born holding Esau's heel, and his name plays on the Hebrew word for heel.

check.q: Which later event do many readers see as the text balancing Jacob's trick on his father?
choices: Laban gives him Leah instead of Rachel in the dark
Rebekah is found at a well
Isaac is nearly offered on Moriah
check.why: In Genesis 29 Jacob is deceived in the dark by a swap, echoing how he deceived Isaac in Genesis 27.

lessons.title: Leah, Rachel and a Night of Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: Jacob's two wives and their children become the twelve tribes, and a night of wrestling gives Jacob and the whole people the name Israel.
reading: In Laban's house Jacob works seven years for Rachel, is given Leah instead, and then works seven more for Rachel. Genesis 29 and 30 tell of the two sisters and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah, and of the children born to each. Leah, the text says, was unloved, and names her sons for her hope that her husband will love her. Rachel is barren for years before Joseph is born. Between them, twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah, are born.

Those twelve sons become the twelve *tribes* of Israel in the rest of the Tanakh: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin. Later, Joseph's two sons Ephraim and Manasseh count as tribes in his place. Jewish parents bless their sons on Friday nights with the words Jacob speaks over those two grandsons in Genesis 48.

After twenty years, Jacob leaves Laban and heads home, afraid of Esau. The night before they meet, Genesis 32 says he is left alone by the Jabbok stream and a man wrestles with him until dawn. The stranger cannot beat him, touches his hip and leaves him limping, and then gives him a new name: *Israel*. The text explains it as "he strives with God." Jacob names the place Peniel, "face of God," and says he has seen God face to face.

Who was the stranger? The text calls him a man. Hosea 12 calls him an angel. Some midrashim say he was Esau's guardian angel. Some modern readers see Jacob wrestling with his own past. The name Israel is then given to Jacob's descendants, and the Tanakh calls them "the children of Israel." The name itself, tradition notes, means struggle. The next morning Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, and weeps.

words.d: the twelve family groups of Israel, descended from Jacob's sons
the new name given to Jacob in Genesis 32, and then the name of his descendants
the daughter of Jacob and Leah, whose story is told in Genesis 34

look.title: Who Wrestled Jacob?
look.text: Genesis 32:25 says "a man" wrestled with him until the breaking of the day. Hosea 12:5 (JPS numbering) says Jacob strove with an angel. A midrash in Genesis Rabbah names the stranger as the guardian angel of Esau. Some modern Jewish readers suggest Jacob was wrestling with his own conscience before facing the brother he had wronged.
look.prompt: Each reading changes what the new name Israel means. Pick one reading and explain what "he strives with God" would mean under it.

check.q: What new name does Jacob receive in Genesis 32?
check.why: The stranger at the Jabbok names Jacob "Israel," which the text explains as striving with God.

check.q: Which two grandsons of Jacob later count as tribes in Joseph's place?
check.why: Genesis 48 has Jacob adopt Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh, and later lists count them as tribes.

check.q: How does the book of Hosea describe the one Jacob wrestled?
check.why: Hosea 12 says Jacob strove with an angel; Genesis 32 itself simply says "a man."

lessons.title: Joseph: A Story With a Shape
lessons.mainIdea: The Joseph story in Genesis 37–50 reads like a short novel, with dreams, a pit, a prison, a palace, and a scene where brothers finally recognize each other.
reading: Genesis 37 begins the longest single story in the book. Jacob loves Joseph best and gives him a special coat. Joseph tells his brothers two dreams in which they bow to him. They hate him, throw him into a pit, and sell him to traders headed for Egypt. They dip the coat in goat's blood and let their father believe Joseph is dead. Many readers note the goat: Jacob once used goatskins to deceive his own father.

In Egypt, Joseph rises in the house of an official, is falsely accused by the official's wife, and lands in prison. There he interprets the dreams of two of Pharaoh's servants. When Pharaoh has dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin ones, Joseph is called from prison to explain them. He predicts seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and Pharaoh puts him in charge of storing grain. Joseph, sold as a slave, becomes the second most powerful man in Egypt.

Scholars often call these chapters a *novella*, a short novel, because the story is long, has one plot, and moves toward a single climax. The climax comes when famine drives the brothers to Egypt to buy grain. They bow before Joseph, as in the dreams, and do not know him. He tests them, hides a silver cup in Benjamin's sack, and waits to see whether they will abandon this brother too. Judah steps forward and offers himself in Benjamin's place.

Then Joseph can hold back no longer. Genesis 45 says he sends everyone out, weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear, and says, "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" The brothers cannot answer. This *recognition scene* is the payoff of the whole story. Jacob's family moves to Egypt, which sets up the book of Exodus. Genesis ends with Joseph's death and his request that his bones one day be carried back to the land.

words.d: a short novel; scholars use the word for the Joseph story because it has one long plot
the moment in a story when characters finally learn who someone really is
Jacob's fourth son, who offers himself in place of Benjamin; the tribe from which David comes

look.title: Joseph Reads His Own Story
look.text: And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
look.prompt: Joseph gives his own reading of the pit, the prison and the palace. Does the narrator ever say this directly, or only Joseph? Why might that matter?

check.q: Why do scholars sometimes call the Joseph story a novella?
choices: Because it is written in Egyptian
Because it is a long story with one plot moving to a single climax
Because it was added to Genesis in the Middle Ages
Because it has no named characters
check.why: A novella is a short novel; Genesis 37–50 has one continuous plot that builds to the recognition scene.

check.q: Who offers himself in place of Benjamin before Joseph reveals himself?
check.why: Judah's speech in Genesis 44 offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, and Joseph then breaks down.

check.q: What detail do many readers connect between Joseph's brothers' trick and Jacob's own trick years before?
check.why: Jacob used goatskins to fool Isaac; the brothers dip Joseph's coat in goat's blood to fool Jacob.

lessons.title: What Archaeology Can and Cannot Say
lessons.mainIdea: Historians place Genesis in the world of the ancient Near East and can describe that world, but they cannot confirm or deny the lives of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
reading: Genesis is set in a real region: Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt. Archaeologists have dug up cities the book names, such as Ur and Haran, and thousands of clay tablets from the second millennium BCE. Those tablets show customs like the ones in Genesis, such as a childless wife giving a servant to her husband so that an heir can be born. The Code of Hammurabi, a Babylonian law collection from c. 1750 BCE, sets out laws about slaves, marriage and injury that later readers compare with the Torah's laws.

What archaeology cannot do is find Abraham. No inscription names him, Isaac or Jacob. Nomadic families leave few traces, and the events are placed long before any writing about Israel survives. The oldest object outside the Bible that names "Israel" at all is an Egyptian stone called the Merneptah Stele, from c. 1208 BCE, and it says nothing about the ancestors. Historians therefore describe the stories as set in a real world, without being able to test them as events.

Scholars also study when Genesis was written down. Most date the written book, in the form we have, to sometime between c. 1000 and c. 500 BCE, with older stories and poems inside it. The oldest surviving copies of Genesis are fragments among the Dead Sea Scrolls, from c. 200 BCE onward. The full Hebrew text used today is preserved in the Masoretic manuscripts of c. 900 to 1000 CE. Jewish tradition holds that the Torah was given to Moses; historians describe the text's growth. This course reports both.

So a careful answer to "Did it happen?" sounds like this. The world of Genesis is real and well known. Its customs and laws fit the second and first millennia BCE. Its people cannot be found or ruled out by digging. What a reader makes of that depends on the reader, and Jewish tradition has never made the value of the Torah depend on a spade.

words.d: the study of the past through objects, buildings and writings dug from the ground
an Egyptian inscribed stone from c. 1208 BCE, the oldest known object outside the Bible to name Israel
ancient manuscripts found near Qumran from 1947 on; they include the oldest copies of Genesis

choices: An Egyptian stone from c. 1208 BCE that names Israel

Describe the customs and cities of the world Genesis is set in
Show that Genesis was written in Egypt

check.why: Fragments of Genesis among the Dead Sea Scrolls, from c. 200 BCE onward, are the oldest copies known.

review.why: Genesis (Bereshit) is first, then Exodus (Shemot), then Leviticus (Vayikra).

choices: A Mesopotamian poem, older than the Bible, with a flood story
A midrash on the tower of Babel
review.why: Gilgamesh is a Mesopotamian epic; its tablet XI tells a flood story that scholars compare with Genesis 6–9.

review.q: Which reading of Eden belongs mainly to Christian tradition rather than Jewish tradition?
choices: A story about choice and its results
A story that connects to Shabbat
A story of original sin entering all human nature
review.why: The doctrine of original sin developed in Christian thought, especially after Augustine; Jewish readers tend to stress choice and responsibility.

review.q: Which of these is a midrash rather than a passage in Genesis?
choices: Sarah laughs at the promise of a son
review.why: The idol story comes from Genesis Rabbah, a midrash collection, and is not in the biblical text.

review.q: On what holiday is the Akedah read in synagogue?
review.why: Genesis 22 is the Torah reading for the second day of Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar is also blown.

review.q: What does the name Israel, given to Jacob, mean according to Genesis 32?
review.why: Genesis 32 explains Israel as striving with God; Ishmael means "God hears" and Isaac plays on laughter.

review.q: What is the climax of the Joseph story?
choices: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers in Egypt
Joseph is thrown into a pit
review.why: The recognition scene in Genesis 45, when Joseph says "I am Joseph," is the moment the whole plot builds toward.

review.q: Which statement about Genesis and archaeology is accurate?
choices: Digs have found Abraham's tomb and his written name
The customs and cities of the region are known, but no find names the ancestors
Archaeology has proven the stories never happened
The oldest copy of Genesis is from Egypt
review.why: Tablets and cities show the world of Genesis, but nothing outside the Bible names Abraham, Isaac or Jacob, either to confirm or deny them.

chapters.title: Exodus: Liberation, Sinai, the Mishkan
chapters.bigQuestion: How does the book of Exodus move from slavery to freedom to law to building, and why has its story been told and sung so far beyond ancient Israel?

story.title: One Song, Two Shores
story.kicker: A song of freedom sung at the edge of a sea, and the same story sung in a field in 1850 by people who had never seen that sea.
paragraphs: The book of Exodus says the people stood on the far shore with the water behind them. Hours before, they had been trapped: Pharaoh's chariots at their backs, the sea in front. Then, the text says, the sea parted, they crossed on dry ground, and the water came back over the army that followed. On the shore, Moses and the people sing. The Torah gives the words of the song in Exodus 15.

Miriam, Moses's sister, takes a hand drum, and the women follow her with drums and dancing. Her line is short: sing to the LORD, for the horse and its rider are thrown into the sea. In Torah scrolls this song is written differently from the rest of the text, in a pattern of short blocks with spaces, like bricks in a wall. A scribe copying it can see the song before reading a word.

Now move nearly three thousand years forward, to a plantation in the American South around 1850. People who have been enslaved gather at night. They cannot read the Hebrew, and most cannot read at all. But they know the story, because preachers have told it. They sing: when Israel was in Egypt's land, let my people go. The song is called "Go Down, Moses," and its Moses is anyone who leads people out.

Harriet Tubman, who guided enslaved people north to freedom, was called Moses by those she helped. When the song was first printed in 1861, it was because a chaplain heard Black refugees from slavery singing it at a Union fort in Virginia. The story of Exodus had become their story, told in their words.

This chapter follows Exodus, called *Shemot* in Hebrew, from slavery to the sea, from the sea to the mountain, and from the mountain to the building of a tent for God to dwell among the people. It also follows the story out of the book: into the Passover Seder, where Jewish families retell it every spring, and into American history, where it became a song of freedom.
story.think: The same story of leaving Egypt is retold at a Seder table and in a spiritual sung under slavery. What does each group of singers need the story to do for them?

lessons.title: Slavery and a Baby in a Basket
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus opens with the descendants of Jacob enslaved in Egypt and with five women whose choices save the baby who will become Moses.
reading: The second book of the Torah begins with a list of names, and its Hebrew title, *Shemot*, means "names." The English title, Exodus, is Greek for "going out." The book picks up where Genesis left off. Jacob's family has grown into a people in Egypt. A new Pharaoh, the text says, did not know Joseph. He fears the Israelites, forces them to build store cities, and makes their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar.

When the people keep growing, Pharaoh orders two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill newborn Hebrew boys. The text says they fear God and refuse. Then Pharaoh orders every boy thrown into the Nile. A woman from the tribe of Levi hides her baby three months. Then she puts him in a basket of reeds sealed with pitch. She sets it among the rushes at the river's edge. His sister watches from a distance.

Pharaoh's daughter comes to bathe, sees the basket, and takes pity on the crying child. The sister steps forward and offers to find a Hebrew nurse, and brings the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter names the boy Moses. Exodus 2 connects the name to a Hebrew verb meaning "to draw out," because she drew him from the water. Scholars also note that the name looks Egyptian, like the ending of the names Thutmose and Ramesses.

Readers have long pointed out that in these first chapters every rescuer is a woman: two midwives, a mother, a sister, and a princess. Jewish tradition names the mother Yocheved and the sister Miriam, and a midrash credits the women of that generation with keeping hope alive. Moses grows up in Pharaoh's house. He kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew and flees to Midian. There he marries and tends sheep.

words.d: Hebrew for "names"; the Hebrew title of the book of Exodus, from its first words
the English title of the second book of the Torah; a Greek word for "going out"
women who help at births; in Exodus 1, Shiphrah and Puah refuse Pharaoh's order

look.title: Five Women and One Basket
look.text: Exodus 1–2 in order: the midwives Shiphrah and Puah refuse to kill the boys; a Levite mother hides her son and then sets him in a basket; his sister stands watch; Pharaoh's own daughter lifts him from the water; the sister arranges for the mother to nurse him. Pharaoh gives orders; the women quietly undo them.
look.prompt: The narrator never says these women were heroes. How does the order of the scenes make the point without saying it?

check.q: What does the Hebrew title Shemot mean?
check.why: Shemot means "names," from the book's opening list of the sons of Israel; Exodus is the Greek title.

check.q: Who does Exodus 1 say refused Pharaoh's order to kill newborn boys?
check.why: Exodus 1:17 says the midwives feared God and did not do as the king commanded.

check.q: How does Exodus 2 explain the name Moses?
choices: It means "son of a king" in Hebrew
It comes from the Nile River's name
Pharaoh's daughter drew him out of the water
check.why: Exodus 2:10 links Moses to a Hebrew verb for drawing out, because he was drawn from the water.

lessons.title: The Name at the Bush
lessons.mainIdea: At a burning bush, Exodus says God calls Moses and gives a name that Jewish tradition treats with great care.
reading: Exodus 3 finds Moses in the wilderness with his father-in-law's sheep, near a mountain the text calls Horeb. He sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. When he turns aside to look, a voice calls his name from the bush. It tells him to take off his sandals, because the ground is holy. The voice says it is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that it has seen the suffering of the people in Egypt. Moses is to go to Pharaoh.

Moses objects five times over two chapters. Who am I? What is your name? What if they do not believe me? I am slow of speech. Send someone else. The text answers each objection, and finally sends his brother Aaron to speak with him. Many readers notice that the Torah's greatest prophet begins by trying to refuse the job.

When Moses asks for a name, the answer in Hebrew is *Ehyeh asher Ehyeh*. JPS 1917 renders it "I AM THAT I AM." Other translations say "I will be what I will be." The text then gives the four-letter name of God. Jewish tradition does not pronounce it. When reading Torah aloud, Jews say *Adonai*, "my Lord," in its place, and in everyday speech many say *HaShem*, "the Name." JPS 1917 prints it as "the LORD" in capital letters, and this course follows that practice.

Rashi reads the name as a promise: I will be with them in this trouble as I will be with them in troubles to come. Some modern scholars read it as a refusal to be pinned down, a name that is really a verb. Christian readers have connected the phrase to lines in the Gospel of John. For a student, the key skill is to see the difference between a name, a title, and a translation of either.

words.d: the mountain of the burning bush in Exodus 3; the Torah also calls the mountain of the covenant Sinai
"my Lord"; the word Jews say in place of God's four-letter name when reading Torah
"the Name"; a respectful everyday way many Jews refer to God

look.title: The Answer to Moses
look.text: And God said unto Moses: 'I AM THAT I AM'; and He said: 'Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel: I AM hath sent me unto you.'
look.prompt: The Hebrew can also be read as "I will be what I will be." How does the meaning shift when the verb is future rather than present? Which reading fits a people about to leave slavery?

check.q: What do Jews say aloud in place of God's four-letter name when reading Torah?
check.why: Jewish tradition does not pronounce the four-letter name; Adonai, "my Lord," is read instead.

check.q: Which of these is one of Moses's objections at the bush?
choices: The sheep will be lost without me
check.why: Exodus 4:10 has Moses say he is slow of speech; the text answers by sending Aaron with him.

check.q: How does Rashi read the name "I will be what I will be"?
choices: As a warning that God will leave the people
As a riddle with no meaning
As a promise to be with the people in this trouble and in troubles to come
As the name of the mountain
check.why: Rashi reads the doubled verb as a promise of presence in present and future suffering.

lessons.title: Ten Plagues and the First Passover
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 7 through 12 tells of ten plagues and a night of departure, and Jewish families still mark that night each year with the Passover Seder.
reading: Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with a demand: let my people go. Pharaoh refuses, and Exodus tells of ten *plagues* that strike Egypt. The Nile turns to blood. Frogs, lice and swarms follow. The cattle sicken and boils break out. Hail, locusts and three days of darkness come. Last, at midnight, the firstborn of Egypt die. Between plagues the text says Pharaoh's heart is hardened, sometimes by Pharaoh and sometimes by God, a detail commentators have discussed for centuries.

Before the last plague, the text gives instructions. Each family is to take a lamb and roast it. They eat it in haste with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. They mark their doorposts with its blood. The text says the plague will pass over those houses. The Hebrew name of the holiday, *Pesach*, comes from that passing over. The people leave so fast their dough has no time to rise. That is why *matzah*, flat unleavened bread, is eaten for the festival. The Torah sets its length at seven days.

Exodus 12 and 13 say the story must be told to children each year. Jewish families do this at the *Seder*, a meal with a set order. It is held on the first night of Passover, and outside Israel on the second night too. The book used is the Haggadah, "the telling." It includes four cups of wine and four questions asked by the youngest. There is a plate with matzah, bitter herbs and other symbols. There are songs. When the plagues are named, a drop of wine is spilled for each one.

Readers have handled the plagues in different ways. The Haggadah's spilled wine is often explained as lessening joy because Egyptians suffered. A midrash has God silence the angels who wanted to sing when the Egyptians drowned. Some scholars compare the plagues to natural disasters of the Nile valley. Others read them as a contest between the God of Israel and the gods of Egypt, each plague striking something Egypt honored. The text itself says the point is that Egypt and Israel will know who the LORD is.

words.d: the ten disasters Exodus says struck Egypt, from the Nile turning to blood to the death of the firstborn
Passover, the spring festival marking the leaving of Egypt; the name means "passing over"
the Passover meal with a set order, at which the story of Exodus is retold from the Haggadah
flat unleavened bread eaten on Passover, because the dough had no time to rise

Because Moses ate it at the burning bush

choices: The book of the Torah after Exodus
The book read at the Seder that tells the Exodus story
A commentary by Rashi on the plagues
The Hebrew name for the Nile

choices: To count the days of the festival
To show a sign to Pharaoh

lessons.title: The Sea and the Song
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 14 and 15 tell of the crossing of the sea and give the oldest-sounding poetry in the book, which Jewish prayer still repeats every day.
reading: After the people leave, Pharaoh changes his mind and sends chariots after them. Exodus 14 says they are caught between the army and the sea. Moses stretches out his hand. A strong east wind blows all night. The people cross on dry ground with water on either side. The Egyptians follow, and the sea returns over them. The Hebrew calls it *Yam Suf*, which JPS 1917 translates as the Red Sea; many scholars think it means "Sea of Reeds."

Then comes the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15. It is a poem, and many scholars believe its Hebrew is among the oldest in the Bible. It repeats ideas in pairs, the *parallelism* found across Hebrew poetry. The horse and rider are thrown into the sea; the deeps cover them. The enemy says "I will pursue, I will overtake." It ends with the LORD reigning forever. At verse 20 Miriam is called a prophetess, and she leads the women with drums.

The song did not stay in the book. Two of its lines, beginning "Who is like unto Thee," are sung in the daily morning and evening prayers. The whole song is read in the morning service. The Shabbat on which Exodus 15 is read each year is called Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of Song. In a Torah scroll the song is laid out in a brick pattern, one of the few passages in the Torah given a special layout.

There is also a tradition about how the song is read. The Talmud, in tractate Sotah, records a debate about how Moses and the people sang. Did he sing a line and they repeat it? Or did they sing together? A midrash says the angels wished to sing as the Egyptians drowned. God stopped them, saying the work of my hands is drowning in the sea. Jewish readers have used that midrash to balance the joy of the song with the cost of the victory.

words.d: the sea the Israelites cross in Exodus 14; JPS 1917 says Red Sea, many scholars say Sea of Reeds
saying one idea twice in two matching ways; the main pattern of Hebrew poetry
the Sabbath of Song, when Exodus 15 is read in the synagogue

look.title: The First Line of the Song
look.text: I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea.
look.prompt: Find the two halves of the line. How does the second half give the reason for the first? Then compare Miriam's line in 15:21, which repeats it almost word for word.

check.q: What is parallelism in Hebrew poetry?
choices: Rhyming the last word of each line
Writing the poem in two columns
Saying one idea twice in two matching ways
check.why: Hebrew poetry pairs ideas, as in "the horse and his rider" and "thrown into the sea"; it does not depend on rhyme.

check.q: Who leads the women with drums after the crossing in Exodus 15?
check.why: Exodus 15:20 calls Miriam a prophetess and says she led the women with drums and dancing.

check.q: Where does the Song of the Sea still appear outside the book of Exodus?
check.why: Lines beginning "Who is like unto Thee" are part of the daily prayers, and the full song is read each morning.

lessons.title: Sinai and the Ten Sayings
lessons.mainIdea: At Sinai, Exodus says the people hear ten sayings, and Jewish, Catholic and Protestant traditions count the same words in three different ways.
reading: In the third month after leaving Egypt, Exodus 19 says the people camp at the foot of Mount Sinai. God tells Moses that if the people keep the covenant they will be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people answer that they will do all that the LORD has spoken. Three days later, the text says, there is thunder, lightning and a thick cloud. A loud horn sounds, and the mountain smokes. Then the words of Exodus 20 are spoken.

Jewish tradition calls these words *Aseret HaDibrot*, the Ten Sayings or Ten Words, rather than ten commandments. It counts them starting from "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt." That first saying is a statement, not an order. The second in the Jewish count joins "no other gods" with the ban on images. Catholic and Lutheran tradition treat the opening statement as an introduction. They join the first two and split the last saying about coveting into two. Most Protestant traditions keep "no other gods" and "no images" as separate commands one and two.

So the same verses give three lists. This is a good example of how a text and its readers work together. The Hebrew text has no numbers in it; each tradition supplies its own. The Sayings appear twice in the Torah, in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, with small differences. The Exodus version says to remember the Sabbath because God rested at creation; the Deuteronomy version says to keep it because you were slaves in Egypt.

Jewish tradition links the giving of the Torah to the holiday of *Shavuot*, seven weeks after Passover. Exodus 19 and 20 are read in the synagogue, and many people stay up all night studying. In many synagogues the congregation stands when the Ten Sayings are read. The Talmud also records a caution. The rabbis removed the Sayings from the daily prayers. They did not want anyone to think these ten mattered and the rest of the Torah did not.

words.d: the Ten Sayings or Ten Words, the Jewish name for what English often calls the Ten Commandments
the mountain where Exodus says the covenant was made and the Ten Sayings were heard
the festival seven weeks after Passover, which Jewish tradition links to the giving of the Torah

look.title: The First Saying
look.text: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
look.prompt: Jewish tradition counts this as the first of the ten. Some Christian traditions call it an introduction. What changes about the whole list if its first item is a reminder of rescue rather than a rule?

check.q: What is the first of the Ten Sayings in the Jewish count?
choices: Thou shalt have no other gods before Me
I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt
check.why: Jewish tradition begins the count with the statement in Exodus 20:2, which is not phrased as a command.

check.q: How does the Deuteronomy 5 version of the Sabbath saying differ from Exodus 20?
choices: It gives slavery in Egypt, not creation, as the reason
It leaves out the Sabbath entirely
It says the Sabbath is on Sunday
check.why: Exodus 20 ties the Sabbath to God's rest at creation; Deuteronomy 5 ties it to having been slaves in Egypt.

check.q: Which holiday does Jewish tradition connect with the giving of the Torah at Sinai?
check.why: Shavuot, seven weeks after Passover, is celebrated as the time of the giving of the Torah, and Exodus 19–20 is read.

lessons.title: The Covenant Code
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 21 through 23 is a collection of laws for daily life, and rabbinic tradition reads even its harshest-sounding lines in a specific way.
reading: After the Ten Sayings, the Torah does not go straight back to story. Exodus 21 to 23 is a block of laws that scholars call the *Covenant Code*, because Exodus 24 calls it the book of the covenant. The laws are mostly case laws: if this happens, then do that. If an ox gores a person, if a fire spreads to a neighbor's field, if someone borrows an animal and it dies. Many of the cases are like ones in the Code of Hammurabi, which is centuries older, and scholars compare them line by line.

The Covenant Code includes laws about slavery, which the text takes for granted as a practice of its world. A Hebrew slave must be freed in the seventh year. Killing a slave is punished. A slave injured by a master goes free. These laws limit a practice rather than end it, and readers from the rabbis to modern historians have noted both the limits and what the text does not do. Describing that honestly is part of reading the book.

One line in Exodus 21 has become famous: eye for eye, tooth for tooth. Rabbinic tradition, in the Talmud's tractate Bava Kamma, reads this as payment for injury, not as injury in return, and Jewish law has followed that reading for two thousand years. Some readers point out that even the plain sense sets a limit: one eye, not a life. The words are the same; the readings differ, and the Talmud's is the one Jewish practice adopted.

The code also returns again and again to the weak. Do not wrong a stranger, it says, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. Do not afflict the widow or the orphan. If you take a poor man's cloak as a pledge, return it by sunset, because it is his only covering. Jewish tradition counts the command to love or not wrong the stranger as the most repeated command in the Torah. The reason given each time is memory: you know what it felt like.

words.d: the block of laws in Exodus 21–23, named from "the book of the covenant" in Exodus 24
a law written as a case: if this happens, then this is what must be done
a tractate of the Talmud on damages, where the rabbis read "eye for eye" as payment

look.title: The Stranger, Three Ways
look.text: Exodus 22 and 23 twice tell the people not to wrong or oppress a stranger, and each time give the reason that they were strangers in Egypt. Rashi explains that a stranger here means someone from elsewhere who lives among you. Ramban adds that the point is not only pity but the memory that God heard the cry of the powerless in Egypt and will hear it again. Modern Jewish groups often quote these verses in debates about immigrants.
look.prompt: Why does the Torah give a memory as the reason for a law, instead of just giving the law? What happens to the law when the memory fades?

check.q: Why do scholars call Exodus 21–23 the Covenant Code?
choices: Because Exodus 24 calls it the book of the covenant
Because it is written in a secret code
Because it was found in the Dead Sea Scrolls
check.why: Exodus 24:7 says Moses read "the book of the covenant" to the people, so scholars use that name.

check.q: How does the Talmud's tractate Bava Kamma read "eye for eye"?
choices: As a command to blind the offender
As payment in money for the injury
As a law only for kings
As a proverb with no legal force
check.why: Rabbinic tradition reads the phrase as compensation, and Jewish law has followed that reading.

check.q: What reason does the Covenant Code give for not wronging a stranger?
choices: Strangers might be angels in disguise
Pharaoh will punish those who harm strangers
You were strangers in the land of Egypt
check.why: Exodus 22 and 23 both give the memory of Egypt as the reason to treat the stranger fairly.

lessons.title: The Golden Calf and the Thirteen Attributes
lessons.mainIdea: While Moses is on the mountain, the people make a golden calf, and the story that follows gives Jewish prayer its most repeated words about mercy.
reading: Moses goes up the mountain for forty days to receive the tablets. Exodus 32 says the people grow afraid that he is not coming back. They press Aaron, who collects their gold earrings and makes a calf. They call it the god that brought them out of Egypt and hold a feast. On the mountain God tells Moses what is happening and offers to destroy the people and start over with him. Moses argues back: what will the Egyptians say, and what about the promise to Abraham?

Moses comes down, sees the dancing, and smashes the tablets at the foot of the mountain. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on water and makes the people drink it. The Levites carry out a punishment, and a plague follows. Then Moses goes back up to plead for the people, and asks to see God's glory. The text says no one can see God's face and live, but God will pass by and proclaim the name.

Exodus 34:6–7 gives that proclamation. Jewish tradition counts thirteen *attributes* of mercy in it. Among them: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness and truth, keeping kindness for thousands, forgiving sin. The rabbis of the Talmud, in tractate Rosh Hashanah, say that God taught Moses these words as a prayer for forgiveness. They are recited on fast days, on Yom Kippur, and when the ark is opened on festivals.

The tradition also pairs the calf with the calendar. According to the rabbis, Moses came down with the second set of tablets on the tenth of Tishrei. That day is Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. So the day of forgiveness in the Jewish year is tied to the story of the worst failure at the mountain. Commentators differ on how guilty the people were and how guilty Aaron was; Rashi, for instance, reads Aaron as stalling for time. The text itself lets Aaron's weak excuse stand without comment.

words.d: the image the people make from their gold in Exodus 32 while Moses is on the mountain
qualities; the thirteen attributes of mercy are qualities of God listed in Exodus 34:6–7
the Day of Atonement; tradition says the second tablets were given on that date

look.title: The Thirteen Attributes
look.text: Exodus 34:6–7 says that the LORD passed before Moses and proclaimed: the LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, full of kindness and truth, keeping kindness for thousands, forgiving wrongdoing and sin, yet not clearing the guilty. Jewish tradition counts thirteen qualities of mercy in these words and recites them on Yom Kippur and fast days.
look.cite: Exodus 34:6–7, summarized from the Jewish Publication Society Tanakh, 1917; Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17b
look.prompt: The passage lists mercy first and only then says the guilty are not simply cleared. Why might the tradition choose to stop its recitation before the harder words?

check.why: Exodus 32 says Aaron collected the gold and made the calf while Moses was on the mountain.

check.q: Where in the Torah are the thirteen attributes of mercy found?
check.why: The attributes come from Exodus 34:6–7, spoken after the golden calf when Moses pleads for the people.

check.q: According to rabbinic tradition, on what day did Moses bring down the second tablets?
check.why: Tradition places the second tablets on the tenth of Tishrei, Yom Kippur, linking forgiveness to the story.

lessons.title: Why Half the Book Is a Tent
lessons.mainIdea: Thirteen chapters of Exodus describe a portable sanctuary in detail, and readers have asked what that emphasis is meant to show.
reading: A student reading Exodus straight through often gets a surprise around chapter 25. The action stops. For seven chapters, God gives Moses instructions for a tent sanctuary, the *Mishkan*, meaning "dwelling place." The instructions cover everything in it. There is an ark of acacia wood covered in gold, a table, a lampstand with seven branches, and an altar. There are curtains, poles, and the clothing of the priests. Then, after the calf story, six more chapters describe the people building it, almost word for word the same.

Why so much detail? Readers give several answers. The text's own answer is in Exodus 25:8: make me a sanctuary that I may dwell among them. The point of leaving Egypt was not just freedom but a people with God's presence in their midst. Some commentators note that the Mishkan story mirrors the creation story. Both are done in stages. Both end with blessing and rest. The Torah uses similar words for finishing each. A people that could not make a calf could make a home.

The workers are named. Bezalel of the tribe of Judah and Oholiab of Dan are called wise-hearted. The text says Bezalel was filled with the spirit of God in skill and craft. Every person is asked to bring gifts, and Exodus 36 says they brought so much that Moses had to tell them to stop. Many readers see a deliberate contrast with the gold earrings collected for the calf.

The Mishkan is the ancestor of the later Temple in Jerusalem and, in a looser way, of the synagogue. The ark that held the tablets gives its name to the *aron*, the cabinet where Torah scrolls are kept today. The seven-branched *menorah* is still a symbol of the Jewish people. When the book ends, the cloud of God's presence fills the tent, and the people know it is time to move when the cloud lifts. Exodus closes not with a battle but with a building.

words.d: "dwelling place"; the portable tent sanctuary described in Exodus 25–31 and 35–40
the ark; in Exodus the gold-covered chest for the tablets, and today the cabinet for Torah scrolls
the seven-branched lampstand of the Mishkan, now a symbol of the Jewish people
the craftsman of the tribe of Judah whom Exodus says led the building of the Mishkan

look.title: Where the Chapters Go
look.cite: Exodus, chapter divisions as printed in JPS 1917
look.prompt: Add up the chapters about the Mishkan. What share of the book is that? If you were editing Exodus, would you keep both the instructions and the building? Why might the text repeat them?

check.why: Mishkan comes from a Hebrew root for dwelling; Exodus 25:8 says the sanctuary is so that God may dwell among the people.

Both are laws about the Sabbath only

lessons.title: The Haggadah: A Book That Retells a Book
lessons.mainIdea: Passover turns the Exodus story into something Jewish families do each year, and the Haggadah has grown over centuries as the script for that night.
reading: The Torah commands that the story of leaving Egypt be told to the next generation, and Jewish tradition built a whole evening around that command. The Seder follows the Haggadah. Its oldest parts come from the Mishnah, edited c. 200 CE. Its full form took shape in the early Middle Ages. The Mishnah, in tractate Pesachim, already lists the four cups, the questions, and the rule that one begins with shame and ends with praise.

The center of the Haggadah is not a reading of Exodus. It is a rabbinic commentary on four verses from Deuteronomy 26 that sum up the story, with verses from Exodus brought in as proof. The Haggadah quotes Deuteronomy's line that "a wandering Aramean was my father." Then it walks through the going down to Egypt, the oppression, the cry, and the rescue. Moses is barely mentioned at all. Many commentators say this is on purpose, so that the credit goes to God and not to a human leader.

The line from the Mishnah that shapes the whole night is this: in every generation a person must see himself as if he personally went out of Egypt. That is why the Seder is done with the body. People lean to one side like free people at a banquet. They taste salt water for tears. They eat bitter herbs, and a sweet paste that stands for mortar. They open the door. Children ask questions because the Torah says the telling begins with a child's question.

The Haggadah is one of the most printed Jewish books. There are thousands of editions with art, commentary and translation. They run from illuminated medieval manuscripts to modern versions that add readings about freedom today. Because the Seder is held at home, not in a synagogue, families often make their own. In the Chicago area, as across the United States, Jewish communities hold public Seders as well. Many invite neighbors of other faiths as guests.

words.d: "the telling"; the book that gives the order and the words of the Passover Seder
the tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud about Passover, source of the Seder's oldest rules
the fifth book of the Torah; its chapter 26 gives the short summary the Haggadah expands

look.title: As If You Went Out
look.text: The Mishnah in Pesachim 10:5 teaches that in every generation a person is obliged to see himself as though he himself had gone out of Egypt, and quotes Exodus 13:8, where a parent tells a child that this is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt. Many Haggadot add that God did not only redeem our ancestors but us with them.
look.prompt: The verse says "for me," even though the speaker was born long after. How does the Seder try to make that sentence feel true? Name two things done at the table that help.

check.why: The Haggadah expands the short summary in Deuteronomy 26 verse by verse, bringing in Exodus verses as proof.

check.q: Why do many commentators say Moses is barely mentioned in the Haggadah?

Because the Haggadah was written in Egypt
Because Moses was not present at the sea
check.why: The traditional explanation is that the Haggadah keeps the focus on God as redeemer.

check.why: Mishnah Pesachim chapter 10 already describes the four cups, the questions and the order of the evening.

lessons.title: Go Down, Moses
lessons.mainIdea: Enslaved African Americans took the Exodus story as their own, and its words became spirituals, sermons and a language of freedom in American history.
reading: Enslaved Africans in the American South heard the Bible mostly by ear, in sermons and songs. Of all its stories, the one they made most their own was Exodus. Slaveholders often preferred verses telling servants to obey. The enslaved sang about a God who heard the cry of slaves and brought them out. In their songs, Egypt was the South and Pharaoh was the master. The Jordan was the Ohio River or death. Canaan was the North or heaven.

The best known of these *spirituals* is "Go Down, Moses." Its verses retell Exodus: Israel in Egypt's land, oppressed so hard they could not stand. The refrain is let my people go. That is Moses's demand to Pharaoh in Exodus 5 and after. The song was first printed in 1861. A chaplain had heard it sung by Black people who had escaped slavery and reached Fort Monroe, a Union army post in Virginia. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried it across the United States and Europe in the 1870s.

Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned many times to lead others north. The people she guided, and the press, called her Moses. Frederick Douglass and later Martin Luther King Jr. drew on Exodus in their speeches. In his final speech in 1968, King said he had been to the mountaintop and seen the promised land. That picture comes from the end of Deuteronomy, where Moses sees the land he will not enter.

Historians describe this as the Exodus story crossing from one people to another. Jewish readers have noticed and honored it; some Haggadot include "Go Down, Moses" or readings from the civil rights movement. The story that Exodus tells about one nation became, in America, a way for another people to name their own bondage and their own hope. The words belong to the Torah; the song belongs to those who sang it.

words.d: religious songs created by enslaved African Americans, many of them retelling Bible stories
an escaped slave who led others to freedom and was called Moses by those she guided
a Union fort in Virginia where "Go Down, Moses" was first heard by the chaplain who printed it in 1861

look.title: One Refrain, Two Books
look.text: In Exodus, Moses stands before Pharaoh and repeats a demand: let my people go, that they may serve me. In "Go Down, Moses," the refrain is the same four words, sung by people in bondage about themselves. Between the verses, the song tells Moses to go down to Egypt's land and tell old Pharaoh to let my people go. The singers were not in Egypt, and their Pharaoh was not a king of the Nile.
look.prompt: When a story is borrowed, what stays the same and what changes? List one thing the singers kept exactly and one thing they changed to fit their lives.

check.q: In the spirituals of enslaved African Americans, what did "Egypt" usually stand for?
choices: The country of Egypt in Africa
check.why: The singers mapped Exodus onto their own lives: Egypt was the South, Pharaoh the master, Canaan freedom.

check.q: Why was Harriet Tubman called Moses?
choices: She wrote a commentary on Exodus
She led enslaved people out of bondage to freedom
She sang in the Fisk Jubilee Singers
check.why: Tubman guided many people north out of slavery, so those she helped compared her to the leader in Exodus.

check.q: Where does the refrain "let my people go" come from in the Torah?
choices: Moses's demand to Pharaoh in Exodus
The first of the Ten Sayings
check.why: Moses repeatedly tells Pharaoh in Exodus 5 and later chapters to let the people go so that they may serve God.

lessons.title: Exodus and the Historians
lessons.mainIdea: Historians can describe the Egypt of the story and note what is missing from the record, but they cannot settle whether the exodus happened as the Torah tells it.
reading: What does the evidence outside the Bible say? Egypt kept many records, and none of them mentions Israelites in slavery, ten plagues, or an army lost in the sea. Historians point out that ancient kings did not record their defeats, and that a group of workers leaving would not have made the royal lists. Still, silence is silence, and it must be reported. The Torah gives no Pharaoh's name, which makes the story hard to pin to a date.

There are hints. Exodus 1:11 says the Israelites built the store city of Raamses. A city by that name was built by Ramesses II, who ruled Egypt c. 1279 to 1213 BCE. The Merneptah Stele, from c. 1208 BCE, names "Israel" as a people in Canaan by then. Many scholars who think some real memory lies behind the story place it in the thirteenth century BCE. Others think the story took shape much later, in the time of the kings or the exile, and grew from smaller memories of people escaping Egypt.

Jewish tradition itself does not depend on the digging. The Torah is read as Torah; the story is retold at every Seder; and the rabbis teach that the point is what the story asks of a people. Some modern Jewish thinkers say that even if the details cannot be recovered, the story is true in the sense that it has shaped a people's life and law for millennia. Others hold firmly that the events happened as written. This course reports the range of views and takes no side.

For a student, the best answer is careful. The world of the story, with brick-making, store cities, a great river, and a powerful king, is Egypt as it was. The exodus itself has no outside witness, for or against. The book's own claim is a religious one: that a God who freed slaves asks that people to remember what slavery felt like. That claim can be described, quoted and studied, whatever a reader decides about the sea.

words.d: a Pharaoh of Egypt, c. 1279–1213 BCE, who built a city named Raamses like the one in Exodus 1:11
a city of warehouses for grain and supplies; Exodus says the Israelites built Pithom and Raamses
living far from home by force; some scholars date the shaping of Exodus to the Babylonian exile
